fournal of the National Finch and Softhill Society: NFSS President's Message, May, 2002 Everyone always seems to want their chil- | dren to have it better than they had it. Can : this also apply to NFSS? The current energetic and devoted Board of Directors seems determined that future NFSS members have it better than past mem- bers. Because of increased computer avail- | ability, this seems to be happening, and in a kinder, gentler, more immediate way. NFSS members now have more readily available information from the expanded web site and newly titled NFSS Journal. They have more immediate access to expert resources on NFSS Ya- hoogroups.com, for day-to-day avian related problems. There is faster board-member-to-board-member communication via the NFSS _ Officer's group use. Pay-pal offers a quicker way to receive member- ship payments and FinchShop revenue, but has some lessons-to- learn. I like that all officers seem to provide, via the NFSS Yahoo groups, on-going input on what they are aiming for, are accomplish- ing, where their problems are, and when they need advice from the board or others. I also like the creative energy that is re-thinking the roles of each officer, elected or appointed, and asking us to give voting rights to all of those individuals who shape and maintain the NFSS. Further, adversaries to bird/animal breeding force us to become more politically astute, active and “politically correct". In response, I particularly like that heretofore quiet members have stepped forward to lead us in ‘protective’ new goals and objectives. In that direction we will be defining a political activist officer's job this quarter. As the weather changes to summer, we must shift our focus from cold/coel weather management to both the pleasure AND the perils summer heat brings to avian culture. Foods spoil sooner, in- sects and preditors are on the prowl, nests are filled with chicks, fledglings are everywhere, banding becomes serious focus, and rival- ries for mates teaches us that even the docile can cause injury when competition for the finest feather takes its primal course. The summer opens us to easier travel to avian events, outdoor bird marts, and, increased caution regarding quarantine, and being on guard for pests and illnesses. Keep the seed cups full! Sally, tington,President

The posi- tion of 3 Vice President and FinchSave Director assembled a FinchSave Committee to begin working on developing the 2002 fFinchSave Program Guidelines. The committee consists of the following individuals: Ms. Ginny Allen, Mr. Harry Bryant, Mr. Roland Cristo, Ms. Carol Heesen, Mr. Vince Moase and the FSS Director Ms. Kerri McCoy. The committee has chosen to include softbilis in the title of the organization. Therefore, the FinchSave Program is officially entitled the Finch and Softbill Save Program. Definition and Purpose: The Nationa! Finch and Softbill Society established the FinchSave program in 1988. Although, thru the years the program requirements have changed the definition and purpose of the program have not. The long-term goal of the Finch and Softbill Save program is to establish a consortium of breeders of finches and softbills dedicated to producing and maintaining a viable cap- tive bred population of finches and softbills in the United States and Can- ada. With tbe recent NFSS incorporation of Region 8 - Canada, we have included Canada in the tong-term goal of the program. The short-term goal of the pragram is to establish consistent breeding success with participating species in the United States and Canada. 2002 Program Requirements: Participants must meet the following requirements in order to participate in the Finch and Softbill Save program: ¢ Participants must be NFSS members in good standing. ¢ Participants must pay a $15 membership fee annually ¢ Tier One participants must agree to open band all offspring with appropriate sized open numbered bands. * Tier Two participants must agree to close band all offspring with appropriate sized closed bands. ¢ Participants must complete quarterly reports ¢ There is no pair limit requirement at this time Species Captain Roles: The 2002 program will continue to incorporate the use of Species Captains. Species Captains are responsible for gathering information from partici- pants, getting birds into participants’ hands, monitoring bloodlines, commu- nicating with participants and assisting participants with any problems that they may have. They will tie in with the Finch and Softbill Save newsletter. Individuals interested in being a Species Captain will be responsible (with the oversight by the Group Manager), in contributing information on their particular species for the newsletter. Species Captains will need to be pro- active and work with participants reqistered with the finch or softbill specie of which they are Captains. The committee will review these again at a later date. 2002 Program Guidelines (what's new): The Finch and Softbill Save Committee has chosen to establish a multi-tier program for Finch and Softbill Save. One of, if not the biggest change that will be made to the 2002 Finch and Softbill Save program will be lifting the requirement for close banding to qualify for registering with the program. This will be achieved through establishing a multi-tier program. In the past, many have voiced an interest in participating in the program but did not close band their offspring. By establishing a multi-tier program we will hopefully reach those individuals who would like to join the program. Tier One: Tier One of the program will lift the reguirement on close banding. The Finch and Softbill Save 2002 Program however requires that Tier One par- ticipants band all their offspring with open (split) numbered bands. You cannot register same species of bird in both Tier One and Tier Two of the program. You must choose either Tier One or Tier Two per bird specie. You may register a certain specie in Tier One and others in Tier Two and vice versa. The participant upon enrollment will make the decision which species will be registered in each tier of the program. Tier Three and Beyond: The Finch and Softbill Save Committee is currently working on incorporating a Tier Three for the Finch and Softbill Save Program. Tier Three will be geared towards those hobbyists who will adhere to strict record keeping, the required use of specific breeding management software and the re- quired trading of bloodlines on a yearly basis. This level of the program is intended for individuals who may be looking to apply for a cooperative breeding program permit from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, or the Canadian Wildlife Service and for those individuals who are very serious about establishing a genetically viable captive bred population of bird spe- cies. More information on Tier Three will be provided at a later date. Breeder Recognition and Breeder of the Year Awards: The 2002 Finch and Softbill Save program will incorporate recognition awards for its participants. Group Managers and the Finch and Softbill Save Committee will assist the FSS Director in choosing worthy participants to award Breeder Recognition awards on a yearly basis. The NFSS Board of Directors will choose a participant to award the Breeder of the Year award with input provided by the F5S committee. To be eligible for such an award you must be able to demonstrate breeding success with your registered specie(s) and have completed ail FSS required quarterly reports. More de- tails on eligibility will be forthcoming. Many have worked hard at establish- ing species in aviculture and, will be honored for doing so. Membership Fee: In order to incorporate a newsletter, and breeder recognition and breeder of the year awards we must have funds. Presently, the NFSS is not in a position financially to fund these program changes. Awhile back a survey was generated to test the waters and the vast majority of individuals had no problem with paying a membership fee to participate in the Finch and Softbill Save program provided the ideas presented were incorporated into the program and that the membership fee paid was used solely for the pro- gram. We have chosen through the help of tbe survey, to set the cost for participation in the program at $15 yearly. All Finch and Softbill Save par- ticipants must pay a $15 yearly membership fee and remain NFSS mem- bers in good standing. Failure to renew your NFSS membership will result in your expulsion from the Finch and Softbill Save Program, The member- ship fee will be mailed in with your FSS application to the FSS Director, made payable to NFSS. Journal of the National Finch and Sofibill Soviet Bird Fever or My Aviary by Paula Hansen, NFSS member On Valentine's Day in 1991 my husband bought me a male canary from a local pet shop. Six months after that my youngest daughter, Kim, took my husband to a restaurant which had a aviary on the outside, built against the building. She told her dad, “that's what mom wants”. As they ate their bur- gers and gazed out the windows, the proprietor, Lee Reynolds, gave my . husband advice. “What ever you build - don't build it cheap!" nernecoate Construction started in November of 1891. The aviary took about 2 4/2 months to build. During this wait my daughter and i found a bird club. We visited club members’ homes, read bird magazines, and frequented the pub- lic library. | read every finch type book | could find. | learned which birds go with which, and the different types of seed and greens to feed. We also learned what were the good weeds in the garden and gathered recipes, ideas and notes. in this picture there are 3 large glass windows originally built with the house. No scenery as our back yard faced the High School loading dock. Zoning for the area wouldn't work for a separate structure and a slab would add to our property taxes. We placed their cages in the room for a week, then opened up the cage doors (using clothes pins to keep them open). We placed the food dishes outside the cages and waited. Slowly each bird left their cage. It took weeks for the societies to build some muscle tone to fly to the highest perch. They never had this type of space. By Feb- ruary the Canaries had built a nest and laid 8 eggs, 6 of which hatched. Now we had 17 birds and guess who had the next clutch? Yup, the zebras. The third year we counted 80 birds in the aviary. Cleaning time each week- end had grown to 4 hours when keeping 80 birds, 2 hours with 40. Cleaning includes squeegying the windows, water is freshened 3 times a day, and seed kept in a 5 Ib feeder which hangs in the center of the aviary. Since then we have kept mixed pairs in the flight, ne more than a 40 birds at one time, one pair per species. Species kept included Hecks Shaft- tails, Chocolate, fawn, and white Societies, normal Button Quail, Coturnix Quail, Blue Capped waxbills, Gold Breasted waxbills, AFA Siskin project birds, red and black headed Gouldians, Java finches, Fire finches, Orange Weavers, Spice finches, Orange Cheeked waxbills, and Diamond doves. We found that the best floor covering to use is pine shavings changed every 2 months or more depending on the population. Our aviary contains 2 florescent fixtures with special UV bulbs. There is a built-in wall heater with it's own thermostat and hardwired into a separate circuit breaker. Also, there is a Circulating fan (usually used for bathrooms) on a timer for hot weather and when it's too dry inside during winter. The fight switch is on the wall behind the curtain and and there is one in the aviary by the exit deor. An outside thermometer for monitoring the aviary temperature hangs on the aviary wall. We also have a mini microphone {RadioShack} mounted to the ceiling of the aviary. You can imagine the noise. In the house is a amplified speaker so we can listen to the birds.
